answer_to_the_commands_question.question: Is the sweep cap enforced per unit or per session? If per session, a repeat of 2 can legitimately exhaust after one — and then the defect is the message, not the arithmetic.
answer_to_the_commands_question.answer: PER SESSION, and the command's second branch is the right one. But it is narrower still: the budget was not exhausted AT ALL. SweepBudget's FIT RULE — documented on the class since it was written — starts a unit only if it could not possibly overrun the sweep cap. With a $0.50 per-unit cap and $0.3453 remaining, no unit could be guaranteed to fit, so it was declined. That is the conservative behaviour the rule exists to provide, and it is a different fact from running out of money.

THE_CAUSE_OBSERVED_NOT_INFERRED.computed_from_the_real_numbers: SweepBudget(cap=0.50); record(0.1547) -> spent 0.1547, remaining 0.3453; can_start(0.50) -> 0.1547 + 0.50 <= 0.50 -> FALSE. The skip is the fit rule, reproduced exactly.
THE_CAUSE_OBSERVED_NOT_INFERRED.and_the_registration_was_impossible_on_a: --max-spend 0.50 --max-spend-sweep 0.50 --repeat 2 needs $1.00 of a $0.50 sweep. EXACTLY ONE UNIT COULD EVER START. My own pre-registration asked for n=2 under caps that made n=2 unreachable, and nothing in the tool said so before the money moved.
THE_CAUSE_OBSERVED_NOT_INFERRED.so_B19_is_closed_as_not_the_defect_it_lo: The repeat logic was never wrong. Three real defects sat behind the wrong word.

results.defect_1_the_message: skip() and sweep_summary both called a fit-rule decline an exhaustion. skip() now distinguishes them and names the remaining budget; the summary reports produced and requested separately — '1 of 2 units ran, 1 skipped — $0.3453 left but no unit could be guaranteed to fit'.
results.defect_2_the_free_check_that_did_not_exi: SweepBudget.units_that_can_ever_start(per_unit_cap) computes the permitted sample before anything is paid, and the CLI warns when the requested sample exceeds it, with both fixes named: raise the sweep cap to $1.00, or lower the per-unit cap to $0.2500. Verified end to end through the CLI, because arithmetic being right proves nothing about whether anyone is told — the distinction that cost four guards today. A warning rather than a refusal, because a deliberately tight cap is a legitimate way to buy 'as much as this money allows'.
results.defect_3_THE_ONE_THAT_MATTERS_MOST: ScenarioRun.skipped was decided by SUBSTRING-MATCHING THE ERROR MESSAGE against ('not applicable', 'sweep budget exhausted'). That is control flow reading English, which non-negotiable 3 forbids in workflow conditions and which nobody had looked for here. Correcting the fit-rule message BROKE IT INSIDE THIS CHANGE: a skipped unit whose message no longer said 'exhausted' silently started counting as a unit that RAN, which would have inflated the denominator of every pass rate in any sweep that hit its cap. It is now a typed flag, was_skipped, set where the skip is decided; the prose match is kept only as a fallback for ScenarioRun objects built directly from an error string, and a test pins that.
results.how_defect_3_was_caught: An existing test failed — tests/test_sweep_budget.py, five cases. I did not go looking for it and would not have found it by reading. That is convention 22 paying for itself in a change that had nothing to do with it.
results.two_of_the_repos_own_tests_were_wrong: Convention 17 applied twice. test_a_skipped_unit_says_why asserted 'sweep budget exhausted' for a budget with $0.10 OF $0.60 STILL IN IT — the test had enshrined the exact confusion B19 turned out to be. test_the_summary_line_reports_what_was_spent pinned the old summary string. Both corrected with the reasoning in a comment, neither weakened.

questions_for_advisor: Defect 3 is a case of non-negotiable 3 — never parse English for control flow — being violated OUTSIDE the workflow conditions it was written about. `_SKIP_REASONS` is the only instance I found, but I found it by breaking it rather than by looking. A sweep for the pattern (control flow keyed on a message's contents) may be worth its own free command; it is the same shape as Convention 28 and would have the same kind of yield.

The pre-spend warning is a WARNING, not a refusal, and I chose that deliberately — a deliberately tight cap is a legitimate way to buy 'as much as this allows'. But my own pre-registration would have proceeded past it, because a warning in a terminal during a background run is a warning nobody reads. If the advisor wants registered runs protected, the stronger form is: a pre-registration naming an n that the caps cannot deliver is a BLOCKED report. That is a protocol change and therefore a ruling.
